categories.label: Architecture & Design
categories.description: How each tool is built internally, its core design philosophy, and its fundamental model of operation.

llamacpp.summary: Pure C/C++ inference library with no external dependencies. Built on the ggml tensor library. Ships as a static/dynamic library (libllama) plus CLI tools (llama-cli, llama-server). Can be embedded directly into other applications.
details: Built on top of the ggml tensor computation library
Zero mandatory external dependencies — compiles on virtually any C++ toolchain
Ships multiple tools: llama-cli (interactive), llama-server (HTTP server), llama-bench, llama-imatrix, llama-quantize, and more
Library-first design: link libllama.so/libllama.a into your own app
No daemon, no background process — run on demand
CPU-first with progressive GPU offloading
Supports multimodal models via libmtmd
Built-in web UI in llama-server

ollama.summary: Go application wrapping llama.cpp (via llama-server). Runs as a background daemon on port 11434. Provides a model registry, a CLI, and an HTTP API. From PR #15122 onwards, delegates all GGUF inference to an upstream llama-server binary.
details: Written in Go; wraps llama.cpp as its core inference engine
Runs as a persistent background daemon (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux, service on Windows)
Exposes HTTP API on localhost:11434
Manages model lifecycle: download, cache, load/unload
As of 2025 PR #15122: uses upstream llama-server binary for all GGUF models
Additional MLX engine for Safetensor-based models on Apple Silicon
Modelfile system for customising system prompts, templates, and parameters
Model registry at registry.ollama.ai

categories.label: Openness & Extensibility
categories.description: License, source accessibility, ability to fork/modify, plugin systems, and how much the tool lets you customize its internals.

llamacpp.summary: MIT licensed, fully open-source. Every aspect of inference is exposed: kernels, quantization routines, sampling algorithms, tensor backends. You can modify, embed, redistribute, or build commercial products on top without restriction.
details: MIT License — maximum permissiveness
All source code on GitHub, including every backend and kernel
Documented process to add new model architectures (HOWTO-add-model.md)
Documented process to add new hardware backends
C API (llama.h) for integration into any language via FFI
Python bindings via llama-cpp-python, Rust via llama-cpp-rs, Swift via swift-llama
Every inference parameter is exposed as CLI flag or API option
GGUF format is open and documented; tools to convert HuggingFace models included

ollama.summary: MIT licensed as a project. However, Ollama intentionally abstracts away llama.cpp internals. Users interact with a curated Modelfile API; the raw inference flags are hidden. Ollama Inc. controls the model registry and release cadence.
details: MIT License on the Ollama repository
Source is available on GitHub
Does NOT expose llama.cpp's raw inference flags to end users
Model registry is controlled by Ollama Inc. — not community-run
Modelfile offers limited customisation (FROM, PARAMETER, SYSTEM, TEMPLATE, ADAPTER)
No documented plugin or backend extension system
llama.cpp attribution controversy: 411+ days before responding to license compliance issue (#3185)
Ollama Inc. is a VC-backed company — commercial incentives may diverge from community
Cannot easily swap or override the inference engine

categories.label: Model Support
categories.description: Which model formats, architectures, and quantization levels are supported by each tool.

llamacpp.summary: GGUF is the native format. Supports 100+ model architectures. Full quantization control from 1.5-bit to 16-bit. Conversion scripts for HuggingFace SafeTensors included. New models typically land within days of release.
details: Native format: GGUF (llama.cpp created and owns this format)
Quantization: Q2_K, Q3_K_S/M/L, Q4_0, Q4_K_S/M, Q5_0, Q5_K_S/M, Q6_K, Q8_0, F16, BF16, IQ1, IQ2, IQ3, IQ4 families
1.5-bit to 8-bit integer quantization + float types
100+ supported model architectures: LLaMA, Mistral, Mixtral, Phi, Gemma, Qwen, Command-R, Grok, BERT, Falcon, BLOOM, and many more
Multimodal: LLaVA, MiniCPM-V, BakLLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, Gemma-3 multimodal
Embedding models: BERT, nomic-embed, E5
Convert HuggingFace models with included convert_hf_to_gguf.py
Split GGUF support for very large models across multiple files

ollama.summary: Uses GGUF via its model registry. Supports a curated subset of popular models. New architectures depend on Ollama maintainers updating their runner (typically 2–10 day lag). Users can import any local GGUF via Modelfile.
details: Format: GGUF (via llama-server internally)
Safetensor models via MLX engine on Apple Silicon
Model registry: 200+ pre-packaged models at ollama.com/library
Quantization choices limited to what Ollama pre-packages (typically Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0)
Import any GGUF from disk: `ollama create mymodel -f Modelfile` with `FROM /path/to/model.gguf`
Import GGUF from HuggingFace: `ollama pull hf.co/org/model`
Support for new architectures typically lags llama.cpp by days to weeks
Modelfile ADAPTER directive for LoRA adapters

categories.label: API & Integration
categories.description: REST API surface, OpenAI compatibility, native library bindings, and how other software integrates with each tool.

llamacpp.summary: llama-server exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API plus additional llama.cpp-specific endpoints. Also provides a full C/C++ library API (llama.h) and Python bindings. Full control over every sampling parameter.
details: OpenAI-compatible: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/models
llama.cpp-specific: /completion, /tokenize, /detokenize, /embedding, /health, /slots
Native C API via llama.h — usable from any language via FFI
Python: llama-cpp-python (llama_cpp.Llama class, OpenAI-compatible server)
Rust: llama-cpp-rs
Swift: swift-llama
Java: llama.java
Sampling parameters: temperature, top-p, top-k, min-p, mirostat, tail-free sampling, typical-p, repeat penalty, frequency penalty, presence penalty
Grammar-based structured output (GBNF grammars)
JSON schema structured output
Tool calling / function calling support
Batch inference support via /v1/completions or server slots

ollama.summary: Clean REST API on port 11434. OpenAI-compatible endpoints for most common operations. Also provides native Ollama-specific endpoints (chat, generate, embed, pull, push, create). Excellent ecosystem integration (LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI SDK).
details: Ollama native API: POST /api/generate, POST /api/chat, POST /api/embed, GET /api/tags, POST /api/pull, POST /api/push, POST /api/create, POST /api/show
OpenAI-compatible: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/models, /v1/responses
Streaming supported on all generation endpoints
Logprobs NOT supported (as of 2025)
Multi-model in-process: can serve embedding + chat model simultaneously
Official SDKs: Python (ollama-python), JavaScript (ollama-js)
Integrates out-of-the-box with: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Dify, Open WebUI, Continue.dev, Cline, AnythingLLM
NOT a library — cannot embed inside another process; requires daemon

categories.label: Hardware Backends
categories.description: Which hardware accelerators and compute backends are supported, and how easy they are to use.

llamacpp.summary: 16+ hardware backends covering virtually every modern compute platform. First-class support for Apple Silicon (Metal), NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (HIP/ROCm), Intel (SYCL, OpenVINO), Vulkan (cross-platform), and more.
details: BLAS / BLIS — CPU general matrix multiply, all platforms
CUDA — NVIDIA GPU (custom kernels)
HIP — AMD GPU via ROCm
Metal — Apple Silicon GPU (first-class citizen)
Vulkan — Cross-platform GPU (AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, etc.)
SYCL — Intel GPU (Arc, Iris Xe)
OpenCL — Qualcomm Adreno GPU (mobile)
CANN — Huawei Ascend NPU
MUSA — Moore Threads GPU
OpenVINO — Intel CPU/GPU/NPU (in progress)
Hexagon — Qualcomm Snapdragon DSP (in progress)
IBM zDNN — IBM Z & LinuxONE
ZenDNN — AMD CPU (Zen architecture)
WebGPU — Browser/WASM context
RPC — Distributed inference across network
CPU+GPU hybrid — offload any percentage of layers to GPU
Vulkan was supported years before Ollama added it (e.g. Vulkan support since 2023; Ollama added ~2025)

ollama.summary: Supports Metal (macOS), CUDA (NVIDIA), and ROCm (AMD). As of 2025, Vulkan added. Hardware detection is automatic on install. Fewer exotic backends than llama.cpp. Windows ROCm requires recent driver versions.
details: Metal — Apple Silicon (auto-detected on macOS)
CUDA — NVIDIA GPU (auto-detected, bundled driver integration)
ROCm / HIP — AMD GPU (Linux only; Windows requires recent drivers as of 2025)
Vulkan — added in recent versions (was delayed vs. llama.cpp by ~2 years)
CPU fallback — always available
Hardware detection is automatic — no build flags needed
No SYCL, CANN, OpenCL, IBM zDNN, or other exotic backends
GPU layer auto-distribution across multiple GPUs in recent versions
Less control over hybrid CPU/GPU layer split than llama.cpp

categories.label: Performance & Benchmarks
categories.description: Inference speed, memory efficiency, throughput, and real-world benchmark data.

llamacpp.summary: Maximum performance when properly tuned. Exposes every performance lever: batch size, thread count, GPU layer count, context management, mmap/mlock, quantization choice. Consistently benchmarks at or near peak hardware capability.
details: Full control: --threads, --n-gpu-layers, --batch-size, --ubatch-size, --mmap, --mlock, --flash-attn
IQ quantization family (IQ1-IQ4) for extreme compression with quality preservation
AVX/AVX2/AVX512/AMX instruction set optimizations for Intel/AMD x86
ARM NEON and RISC-V vector extensions for mobile/ARM
Custom CUDA kernels — not relying on generic cuBLAS
Flash Attention support (--flash-attn flag)
KV cache quantization (--cache-type-k, --cache-type-v)
Batched inference (--parallel) for multi-request throughput
Benchmarks (RTX 4090): ~334 tokens/s on LLaMA 3.2:3b (llama.cpp raw)
Speculative decoding support for faster generation

ollama.summary: Very good performance out of the box with sensible defaults. Since delegating to llama-server (PR #15122), the raw inference speed gap with llama.cpp has narrowed significantly. Cannot match hand-tuned llama.cpp at high concurrency or exotic hardware.
details: Comparable single-request inference speed to llama.cpp since adopting llama-server
Automatic GPU utilization — no tuning needed for typical use cases
Multi-model in-memory management: hot-swaps models based on demand
Context window managed per Modelfile (num_ctx parameter)
Limited concurrency tuning (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL env var)
Cannot set raw llama.cpp flags like --flash-attn, --ubatch-size per request
Memory management handled automatically — less predictable under load
Benchmarks at parity with llama.cpp for simple single-request workloads
Performance gap becomes visible at 50+ QPS or with exotic quantization

categories.label: Configuration & Control
categories.description: Granularity of control over sampling, generation, context, and runtime parameters.

llamacpp.summary: Maximum control. Every sampling algorithm, context parameter, rope scaling factor, KV cache setting, and hardware tuning knob is directly accessible via CLI flags or API parameters.
details: 40+ CLI flags for generation and sampling control
Sampling: temperature, top-p, top-k, min-p, mirostat (v1/v2), typical-p, tail-free sampling
Repetition: repeat-penalty, repeat-last-n, frequency-penalty, presence-penalty
Context: --ctx-size, --rope-freq-base, --rope-freq-scale, YaRN RoPE scaling
Memory: --mmap, --mlock, --cache-type-k, --cache-type-v, --cache-reuse
Execution: --threads, --threads-batch, --batch-size, --ubatch-size, --flash-attn
Multi-GPU: --tensor-split, --split-mode (layer, row, none), --main-gpu
Grammar-constrained output with GBNF grammar files
System prompt, chat template, and BOS/EOS token override
Slot-based API for multi-user concurrent sessions

ollama.summary: Convenient but constrained. Parameters accessible via Modelfile PARAMETER directives or API 'options' object. Key llama.cpp-specific flags (RoPE scaling, KV cache type, per-request thread count) are not exposed.
details: Modelfile PARAMETER: num_ctx, temperature, top_p, top_k, repeat_penalty, seed, stop, num_predict, num_gpu, num_thread, mirostat, mirostat_eta, mirostat_tau, tfs_z, typical_p
API 'options' object mirrors Modelfile parameters
Cannot set per-request rope scaling or YaRN parameters
No KV cache type override (--cache-type-k/v hidden)
No --flash-attn flag exposed
No per-request ubatch-size or batch-size
Context size change requires creating a new Modelfile variant
keep_alive parameter controls how long model stays in memory
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS env vars for server-level tuning

categories.label: Deployment Flexibility
categories.description: How each tool can be deployed: embedded, server mode, CLI, Docker, mobile, production environments.

llamacpp.summary: Maximum deployment flexibility. Can be compiled for any target with a C++ toolchain: desktop, server, mobile (Android, iOS), embedded, and browser (WebAssembly). Library mode enables embedding into existing binaries.
details: Library mode: link libllama into any application
CLI mode: llama-cli for interactive or batch inference
Server mode: llama-server provides OpenAI-compatible HTTP API
Docker: official images (full/light/server variants)
Android: documented build process, termux support
iOS/macOS: XCFramework for Swift integration
Browser: WebGPU/WASM port
Production: single static binary llama-server, easy to containerize
RPC backend: distribute inference across multiple machines
No runtime dependency — ships as a standalone binary

ollama.summary: Excellent for server/desktop deployment. Signed installers for macOS/Linux/Windows. Runs as a system service. Docker image available. Not suitable for embedded use (requires Go runtime, daemon architecture).
details: macOS: DMG installer, auto-starts as launchd service
Linux: install script, systemd service, available in some package managers
Windows: EXE installer, runs as Windows service
Docker: official docker image (ollama/ollama)
Kubernetes: community Helm charts available
NOT embeddable as a library — requires daemon architecture
NOT suitable for mobile or browser deployment
REST API enables polyglot clients (any language can call it)
Remote access: set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 to expose on network
Multi-model server: handles multiple concurrent model requests

categories.label: Community & Ecosystem
categories.description: GitHub stars, contributor count, release cadence, and the ecosystem of tools built on top.

llamacpp.summary: The foundational infrastructure of the local LLM world. Nearly every local inference tool (Ollama, LM Studio, Jan AI, text-generation-webui, koboldcpp) is built on llama.cpp. 2000+ contributors, weekly releases, extremely active development.
details: ~123k GitHub stars, ~21.5k forks
2000+ total contributors
~78 commits per week (as of mid-2025)
Rolling releases — multiple per week, no formal stable track
Foundation for: Ollama, LM Studio, Jan AI, koboldcpp, text-generation-webui, and more
Georgi Gerganov (lead) is extremely responsive in issues and PRs
Weekly changelog via GitHub releases
Active discussions forum on GitHub
GGUF format co-created with community and widely adopted

ollama.summary: Most starred local LLM project on GitHub (~178k). Large user community drawn by ease of use. Ecosystem of UI wrappers (Open WebUI) and framework integrations. Corporate-backed but active. New model support sometimes lags llama.cpp.
details: ~178k GitHub stars, ~17.3k forks
500+ contributors (more concentrated on core team)
Structured versioned releases (e.g. v0.32.8)
Backed by Ollama Inc. (VC-funded)
Official SDKs: Python and JavaScript
Major integrations: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Open WebUI, Dify, AnythingLLM, Continue.dev, Cline, Cursor
Ollama model library with 200+ pre-packaged models
Very large user community (forum.ollama.com, Reddit, Discord)

categories.label: Limitations & Trade-offs
categories.description: What each tool sacrifices in exchange for its design goals. Honest assessment of pain points.

llamacpp.summary: Power comes at the cost of UX complexity. Requires compilation from source for best performance. No curated model registry. No automatic model lifecycle management. Steep learning curve for new users.
details: No GUI — pure CLI and HTTP server
Compilation required for optimal performance (right CPU flags, GPU backend)
No curated model registry — user must find and download GGUF files from HuggingFace
No automatic model download/update management
Rolling release cadence means no 'stable' version guarantee
API surface evolves rapidly — breaking changes possible
Documentation scattered across README, wiki, and discussions
No built-in multi-model hot-swap (one model per server instance)
Requires understanding of quantization tradeoffs (Q4_K_M vs IQ3_XXS etc.)

ollama.summary: Convenience is traded for control. Cannot access llama.cpp internals. Model registry is proprietary and curated by Ollama Inc. License attribution controversy. Commercial entity interests may diverge from community needs.
details: Intentionally hides llama.cpp flags — many knobs inaccessible to users
Model registry controlled by Ollama Inc. — not community-governed
Support for new architectures lags llama.cpp by days to weeks
Daemon architecture adds complexity (process management, port conflicts)
Cannot embed as a library in another binary
License attribution controversy: 411+ days to respond to compliance issue (#3185)
VC-backed company — future monetization or licensing changes possible
Limited Vulkan support history (years behind llama.cpp)
Modelfile customization is limited compared to raw llama.cpp flags
Windows ROCm support requires latest drivers — compatibility can be fragile

verdict.summary: llama.cpp is the foundational inference engine that powers the local LLM ecosystem — including Ollama itself. It provides maximum control, hardware coverage, and extensibility at the cost of user experience complexity. Ollama wraps llama.cpp in a polished developer experience optimized for ease of use: model management, auto-hardware detection, and ecosystem integration. The 'closed environment' criticism of Ollama is accurate in a specific sense: Ollama intentionally abstracts away llama.cpp's internals, limiting fine-grained control, and its model registry is controlled by a VC-backed company rather than the community.
use_llamacpp_when: You need to embed inference directly inside your application (library mode)
You need exotic hardware backends (Vulkan, SYCL, Ascend, IBM Z, WebGPU)
You need fine-grained control over quantization, KV cache, RoPE scaling, or sampling
You need access to cutting-edge models on the day they release (before Ollama packages them)
You are building production inference at 50+ QPS and need to tune every parameter
You are targeting mobile, WASM/browser, or embedded Linux
You value not depending on a VC-backed company's model registry
use_ollama_when: You want a model running in under 5 minutes with zero configuration
You are building a prototype or local RAG application
Your team needs a shared LLM service on a local network
You want seamless integration with LangChain, LlamaIndex, Open WebUI, or similar frameworks
You are running a home lab and want models to auto-start as a service
Ease of model management (pull, list, delete) matters more than raw performance tuning
Your GPU is NVIDIA or Apple Silicon and you do not need exotic backends
verdict.openness_verdict: Both tools are MIT-licensed and open-source. However, 'openness' in practice differs significantly. llama.cpp exposes every internal mechanism; contributing a new model architecture or backend has a documented path. Ollama's openness is at the application layer — the source is visible, but the inference engine internals are hidden from users. The Ollama model registry is proprietary, and the license attribution controversy (GitHub issue #3185, unresolved for 411+ days) raised legitimate questions about Ollama's relationship with the open-source community it is built upon.
